content: National or regional centers of excellence, staffed by highly trained local professionals, are essential for providing ongoing support to other service providers after international assistance has concluded. This model has demonstrated success in numerous regional training centers and plays a critical role in advancing prosthetics and orthotics services. The costs associated with prosthetics and orthotics services extend beyond human resources, components, and materials. To ensure high-quality service delivery, five primary cost categories must be considered and adequately funded: training human resources, service providers, service users, national monitoring (recurrent costs), and service establishment (investment costs). Each of these categories requires detailed financial analysis to understand their implications, as they may necessitate different funding mechanisms. Service Establishment Establishing prosthetics and orthotics service units and systems requires significant capital investment in infrastructure and equipment, such as buildings, tools, and machinery. While these are typically one-time investments, ongoing maintenance, repairs, and replacements due to wear and tear must also be budgeted. These costs are often included in the operational expenses of service providers. Service establishment is usually funded by governments, non-governmental organizations (NGOs), or private investors. In cases of private establishment, financing may involve loans, with interest and repayments factored into the service provider's costs. Training Human Resources Prosthetics and orthotics services depend on well-trained, qualified professionals. Substantial and continuous financial investment is required to ensure an adequate workforce and to provide ongoing professional development (CPD). Training is often conducted in institutions separate from regular service providers, with funding sources differing accordingly. Clinical placements are typically supervised by service providers linked to educational institutions. Training costs include expenses for facilities (lecture rooms and practical training areas), tools and equipment, training materials, personnel (lecturers and clinical supervisors), and allowances for users involved in practical training. In countries without local training institutions, costs for training abroad—such as tuition, travel, accommodation, and allowances—must be considered. These expenses are sometimes covered by scholarships from employers, governments, civil society organizations, or donors. Service Providers The operational costs of service providers include regular expenses necessary for delivering services. These may encompass material costs (including taxes, procurement charges, and shipping), personnel costs, utilities (e.g., electricity, water, internet), maintenance of buildings and equipment, depreciation, government taxes, loan repayments, and external services provided by healthcare professionals. In private services, providers typically set prices to generate profit, which must be accounted for in cost calculations. Public services should also include salaries and infrastructure costs in their calculations to ensure fair competition with private providers. Stakeholders can estimate the cost of complete treatments for specific conditions, which is crucial for policy advocacy and funding efforts. Service Users The personal expenses incurred by users when accessing services, as well as their loss of earnings, must be considered in the overall cost of service delivery. These expenses may include travel costs (sometimes requiring specialized transport), accommodation, increased meal costs, loss of income, inability to perform household or community tasks, costs for accompanying persons, and childcare expenses. In low-income settings, user costs may exceed the actual service delivery costs and pose significant barriers to access. Subsidizing these costs for at-risk populations can improve accessibility. National Monitoring Monitoring prosthetics and orthotics services ensures they meet population needs and adhere to established standards and regulations. This is typically the least expensive cost category if a well-planned system is in place. Monitoring is usually funded publicly, though tasks may be delegated to NGOs. Costs may include a dedicated office or unit for monitoring and personnel for coordination, regulation enforcement, audits, and evaluations. Economic Benefits Prosthetics and orthotics services yield both direct and indirect economic benefits for individuals, families, communities, and nations. These services are not merely costs but investments with significant social and economic returns. Timely interventions reduce long-term costs by preventing secondary health conditions and enabling individuals to become more independent and productive. This reduces the financial and caregiving burden on families and communities, decreases healthcare expenditures, and allows individuals to return to work or education, contributing to economic growth. At the national level, these benefits accumulate, reducing social welfare costs and increasing tax revenues. Investments in prosthetics and orthotics services also stimulate job creation and economic activity, particularly in countries with prosthetics and orthotics industries. Ensuring Cost-Effectiveness Cost-effectiveness in prosthetics and orthotics services ensures responsible use of funds, making services more affordable and accessible. Efficiency is essential for equitable service delivery. Measures to improve cost-effectiveness include setting realistic treatment goals, adopting cost-effective technologies and materials, ensuring the durability of devices, providing maintenance and repair services, reducing waste, and optimizing staff training and specialization. Governments can further reduce costs by waiving import taxes on components and materials and value-added taxes on services. Decentralization can also enhance cost-effectiveness by reducing user expenses and improving service accessibility.
